ch15-l03-teaching-01:
Why does the uterine lining need a continuing signal?

Implantation attaches a blastocyst to the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus. The conceptus is the developing organism together with its associated membranes. That attachment occurs in tissue whose condition is controlled partly by hormones. To explain why the lining remains in place, start with what normally happens after ovulation.

The ovarian follicle that released the oocyte changes into the corpus luteum, a temporary hormone-producing structure in the ovary. Luteinizing hormone, or LH, from the anterior pituitary helps bring about ovulation and supports this ovarian structure. The corpus luteum releases progesterone and some estrogen. Progesterone helps maintain a secretory, well-supplied endometrium suitable for early development.

A hormone is a chemical message carried to responsive tissues. In this pathway, the ovary is the source of progesterone and the uterine lining is one of its targets. Their locations are different. Progesterone is not the lining itself, and the corpus luteum is not part of the blastocyst.

Without pregnancy-associated support, corpus-luteum activity declines. Its progesterone and estrogen output falls, and the endometrium loses the hormonal support that helped maintain it. Menstrual shedding follows. The important change is a fall in support, not a claim that the body suddenly contains no estrogen or progesterone anywhere. Early pregnancy needs to maintain the ovarian structure beyond its usual short period of activity.
ch15-l03-teaching-02:
Follow one signal to the next

Trophoblast is the outer cell layer of the blastocyst. As implantation develops, tissue derived from that layer releases human chorionic gonadotropin, abbreviated hCG. In the early-pregnancy pathway, hCG travels through maternal blood and acts on the corpus luteum in the ovary. It helps keep that structure active, so the corpus luteum continues releasing progesterone and estrogen.

Read the steps in this order: trophoblast-derived tissue releases hCG; hCG supports the corpus luteum; the corpus luteum releases progesterone and estrogen; those ovarian hormones support the endometrium. The first hormone stimulates a tissue that produces further hormones. hCG does not change into progesterone, and it is not another name for it.

A target responds because it has functioning receptors, molecular structures that recognize the signal and begin a response. Having hCG in the blood and having responsive luteal cells are separate requirements. If a stated model makes the corpus luteum unable to respond, the normal downstream support cannot simply be assumed from the hCG concentration.

As the placenta develops, it becomes an increasingly important hormone-producing tissue. Production of progesterone shifts toward the placenta during the first trimester. Placental estrogen production also becomes substantial as pregnancy continues. Because the source of hormonal support changes, a fall in hCG from its early peak need not mean that progesterone support has ended.

The source figure below connects the changing sources above with hormone patterns below. Locate the ovary and placenta in each upper panel. Then follow the labelled hCG, progesterone and estrogen curves across the trimesters. Read each curve's change through time; the vertical axis has no numerical scale, so it cannot give an exact concentration or a reliable numerical comparison between different hormones.

This textbook illustration is a simplified summary. The change toward placental progesterone production begins during the first trimester; it is not a switch that waits until the second trimester starts. The diagram's broad panels, arrow widths and caption should not be used as exact timing or as proof of an exclusive hormone source at every moment. The declining hCG curve also remains above zero.
ch15-l03-teaching-03:
A hormone result has limits

Many urine pregnancy tests detect hCG. In the normal early-pregnancy pathway we have just traced, trophoblast-derived tissue provides that signal. Measuring the signal is different from observing the embryo or its location. Detectable hCG alone does not show that implantation is in the usual uterine location or establish that development is proceeding normally.

The teacher source describes trophoblast as the only possible source of hCG. That is too absolute: small amounts of hCG can also occur outside pregnancy. Calling hCG a pregnancy-associated signal describes its role in the normal pathway and why pregnancy tests measure it. That label does not prove that a particular detected amount came from a normally located pregnancy. For this course, separate the biological pathway from the limits of a measurement. A stated laboratory result establishes what was detected in the sample; stronger conclusions require other evidence. Interpretation of a person's result belongs with a qualified health professional.

Apply the same care to a hormone graph. First identify the substance on each curve and the time scale. Describe what changes before proposing a cause. Then use the taught source–target relationship to explain how the pattern is possible. A schematic of typical trends is not an individual person's measured record.

The developing conceptus therefore has an early way to influence its environment: its signal supports an ovarian hormone source, which in turn supports the uterine lining. Later placental production changes the dependence on that ovarian source. We will next examine changes within the embryo itself as its cells become organized into tissue-forming layers.

The optional textbook filter also includes earlier fertilization questions and later questions on the amniotic cavity and germ layers. Revisit the earlier questions as review; return to the later ones after the matching teaching rather than assuming all belong to this hormone pathway.
ch15-l03-worked:
Worked example

Explain two curves that move differently

Use Figure 15.5 above. After the red hCG curve reaches its early high point, it declines while the blue progesterone curve remains elevated. A learner concludes, “Less hCG must mean that all progesterone support has stopped.” Does the evidence support that conclusion?

  1. Read the labels first. Red represents hCG and blue represents progesterone. They are different hormones, so a decrease in one is not automatically a decrease in the other.
  2. Describe the observation. The red curve falls from its peak. The blue curve does not fall to zero with it. No numerical concentration can be read because the vertical axis is unnumbered.
  3. Explain the early relationship. hCG supports the corpus luteum, and that ovarian structure secretes progesterone. hCG is an upstream signal rather than progesterone itself.
  4. Include the changing source. The developing placenta increasingly provides progesterone. Continued placental production can support the lining while hCG is lower than at its early peak.
  5. Check the conclusion. The claim that all progesterone support has stopped is inconsistent with the displayed blue curve and ignores the placental contribution. This schematic cannot establish the health of an individual pregnancy.

Now change a condition in a classroom model: hCG is present, but the corpus luteum's receptors cannot respond during the stage when ovarian support matters. Detecting hCG would no longer be enough to infer a normal luteal response. Trace the stated limitation through the chain before predicting the next hormone's effect; do not assume that a later placental contribution is already fully available.
ch15-l04-teaching-01:
What changes when cells form germ layers?

During cleavage, cell number increased, and a blastocyst developed a cavity, inner cell mass and outer trophoblast. Those events prepared different cell populations, but they did not yet make the full range of body tissues. The embryo now needs cells arranged in positions from which different tissues can develop.

During gastrulation, cells move and reorganize to establish three primary germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Cells in the embryonic disc move inward and spread into new positions. Some establish the inner endoderm; others form mesoderm between that inner layer and cells remaining at the surface, which become ectoderm. The resulting three-layer embryo is called a gastrula. A germ layer is an early tissue-forming cell population; “germ” here does not mean a microbe. Ecto- suggests outer, meso- middle and endo- inner. The names help orient the embryonic layers, not locate every resulting tissue in an adult.

In human development, gastrulation begins in the third week after fertilization. An earlier two-layer embryonic disc, a flattened arrangement of early embryonic cells, forms during the second week. The textbook's p. 511 sequence and the teacher's week-two heading compress these changes; distinguish that earlier disc from the three definitive germ layers formed through gastrulation. This timing is counted from fertilization, not from the clinical dating of a pregnancy.

Read the schematic below as a summary of the resulting layers. A identifies ectoderm, B mesoderm and C endoderm. Compare the representative tissues written inside each band. The gaps separate labels for readability; they are not body cavities. The figure does not show the cell movements or the actual three-dimensional shape of a human embryo.

Gastrulation is therefore a change in organization and developmental pathways, rather than simply another increase in cell number. The three layers then participate in morphogenesis, the development of body form and structures. Later folding and movement bring their descendants into complex arrangements.
ch15-l04-teaching-02:
Follow tissue identity rather than adult position

Ectoderm gives rise to the epidermis, the outer cellular layer of skin, and to the nervous system. A spinal cord lies inside the body but still has an ectodermal origin. The layer's embryonic position does not mean that all of its descendants remain on the adult surface. Hair, nails and tooth enamel are other examples in the textbook's source list.

Mesoderm contributes to muscle, bone and other connective tissues, as well as blood, heart and blood vessels, kidneys and many reproductive structures. Connective tissue supports, joins or surrounds other tissues; bone, cartilage and blood are specialized examples. The dermis, the deeper connective-tissue part of the skin, is a different tissue from the epidermis.

Endoderm contributes much of the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory passages, along with important glandular tissues in associated organs such as the liver and pancreas. Epithelium is a closely packed cell layer covering a surface or lining a space. Naming an epithelial lining is more precise than saying that every part of an organ comes from endoderm.

Use the figure's examples to check the distinctions. Nervous tissue and epidermis share the A lineage despite different adult positions. Muscle and blood belong with B. Digestive and respiratory epithelial linings belong with C. An organ combines tissues that can come from different germ layers, so “inside the body” is not a sufficient classification rule.
ch15-l04-teaching-03:
How can related cells do different jobs?

Differentiation is the process through which cells become specialized in structure and function. For example, muscle cells develop machinery for contraction while nerve cells develop structures used for communication. They generally retain the same inherited genome, the complete set of genetic information, rather than acquiring a completely new chromosome set for each job.

What changes is how cells use that information. Gene expression means using the information in a gene to make functional products. Different patterns of gene expression, together with signals from surrounding cells and tissues, help cells take different developmental paths. Establishing cell positions during gastrulation matters because position influences which signals cells encounter.

Keep the processes connected but distinct. Cleavage divides the early structure into more cells. Gastrulation reorganizes cells into tissue-forming layers. Differentiation develops specialized cell types, and morphogenesis produces the shape and organization of structures. These processes interact during development; they are not four interchangeable names for cell division.

When a question names an organ, look for the particular tissue it asks about. Intestinal smooth muscle and intestinal epithelial lining have different functions and origins even though they lie beside each other. A developmental change affecting one contribution need not affect the other identically. Do not turn a tissue-origin explanation into a diagnosis or a prediction that every tissue from that germ layer must be damaged.

The embryo's own layers are also different from the tissues and membranes that support it. Having explained its tissue-forming organization, we will next examine the surrounding support structures and what each contributes.

If the optional textbook filter shows hCG or broader developmental-timeline questions, keep their topic and page in view. They are cross-topic practice. The tissue-origin teaching here is supported by Figure 15.7 on printed p. 513; support membranes and organ development are treated next.
ch15-l04-worked:
Worked example

One skin sample contains several tissue origins

An illustrative tissue record names epidermal cells, deeper dermal connective tissue and sensory nerve cells in the same sample of skin from the trunk. A learner assigns the whole sample to ectoderm because skin is on the outside. Evaluate that claim by classifying each named tissue.

  1. Identify the tissue, not just the organ. Epidermis is the outer cellular covering. Its ectodermal origin fits the A examples in the schematic.
  2. Distinguish the deeper support tissue. Dermal connective tissue belongs with mesodermal support tissues in this classroom model. Calling it skin does not make it epidermis.
  3. Classify the nerve cells by function and lineage. They are nervous tissue, so they have ectodermal origin even though they extend beneath the surface.
  4. Check the claim against all the evidence. The sample includes ectodermal and mesodermal contributions. The location of the organ did not establish a single origin for everything in it.

Use the same method on another organ: first name the tissue, then find its developmental contribution. A passage lined with epithelium can also have muscle and connective tissue in its wall. The fact that its lining has one origin does not assign that origin to all the surrounding tissues.

There is no need to invent a new genome for each cell type to explain this diversity. Cells can specialize through different use of shared genetic information and developmental signals. The germ-layer classification describes developmental relationships, while differentiation explains how specialized cell structure and function emerge.
